before.evidence_summary: The opening defines the central problem as securing the Revolution's achievements through peace, tranquillity, and durable stability.
The text argues that Bonaparte's regime ended the Revolution by resolving within two years the issues that had divided France, while sacrificing most principles of 1789.
Victorious peace is treated as necessary to settle the new government and end the revolutionary war.
The chapter closes with war ended, political strife eliminated, religious freedom restored, and contemporaries celebrating the Revolution's burial.

after.evidence_summary: A Seine-et-Oise commissioner illustrates rural attachment to equality,abolition of dues and new property, alongside desire for priests,peace and calm. The regional report is illustrative rather than proof of uniform national attitudes.
The text argues that Bonaparte's regime ended the Revolution by resolving within two years the issues that had divided France, while sacrificing most principles of 1789.
Victorious peace is treated as necessary to settle the new government and end the revolutionary war.
The chapter closes with war ended, political strife eliminated, religious freedom restored, and contemporaries celebrating the Revolution's burial.

field_changes.before: The resurgence was real but temporary and dependent on crisis; its rhetoric and measures revived fears of Year II and enabled an anti-Jacobin reaction.
field_changes.after: The resurgence was real but did not command a parliamentary majority. Wartime emergency and memories of Year II magnified fear; Sieyes’s containment served his own executive project. Rejection of Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion marks the limit of renewed emergency government.

field_changes.before: Jourdan conscription law, forced loan, and Law of Hostages
field_changes.after: Forced loan and Law of Hostages in1799: coercion and Consular repeal

field_changes.before: The coercive 1799 measures used to mobilize manpower and money and repress resistance, together with their political association with the Terror.
field_changes.after: The forced loan placed punitive wartime assessments on the rich as foreign resources became inadequate. The Law of Hostages authorized collective punishment against relatives of émigrés and nobles without proof of responsibility. Their perceived return to Terror politics helped provoke reaction; Bonaparte repealed both measures to reassure property holders and western insurgents.

field_changes.before: The measures answered a military emergency but were punitive, recalled Year II, broadened arbitrary power, and helped provoke resistance and fear among propertied citizens.
field_changes.after: These two civil emergency measures were repealed after Brumaire. This requirement expressly excludes a claim that the Jourdan conscription law was repealed: recruitment belongs to a separate military requirement. Distinguish the hostage law’s arbitrary liability from the loan’s fiscal burden.

after: Bonaparte--repeal of hostage law and forced loan

before.evidence_summary: Full activation of the Jourdan law and a punitive forced loan are presented as a new mass mobilization funded from domestic resources.
The Law of Hostages permits detention and property penalties without proven responsibility and appears to announce a return to terror.
Brumaire rapidly repeals the hostage law and forced loan as part of reassuring property holders.

after.evidence_summary: The forced loan on wealthy citizens met urgent domestic war-finance needs when foreign resources were no longer sufficient.
The hostage law permitted detention and property penalties against designated relatives without demonstrated responsibility,evoking an extension of Terror.
Repeal of the hostage law was publicized while the new regime negotiated western pacification.
The hostage law and forced loan were rapidly abolished; a moderate proportional surtax replaced the loan.

field_changes.before: Military recovery against the Second Coalition in late 1799
field_changes.after: Military crisis,recovery,and disintegration of the Second Coalition

field_changes.before: French victories in the Batavian and Helvetic republics that reversed the emergency, weakened the coalition, and created favorable conditions for constitutional change.
field_changes.after: The defeats of1799,Novi and Joubert’s death intensified political crisis; recovery in the Netherlands and Switzerland changed the balance. Austrian and Russian rivalry,failed joint strategy,and PaulI’s withdrawal then broke the coalition advantage and opened Bonaparte’s military and diplomatic opportunity.

field_changes.before: The victories are treated as a rapid strategic reversal that restored confidence and enabled Sieyes to move against the existing constitution.
field_changes.after: French recovery mattered,but allied division and selfish aims also explain the opening. Do not present victory as uninterrupted or attribute all coalition failure to Bonaparte.

before.evidence_summary: French forces defeat the Anglo-Russian invasion in the Netherlands and drive divided Russian forces from Switzerland.
The improved military position creates the moment Sieyes believes suitable for an executive-strengthening coup.

after.evidence_summary: Joubert’s death and defeat at Novi,followed by coalition landings,deepened military and political emergency.
French forces defeat the Anglo-Russian invasion in the Netherlands and drive divided Russian forces from Switzerland.
The improved military position creates the moment Sieyes believes suitable for an executive-strengthening coup.
Allied territorial interests and Austrian conduct obstructed coordinated exploitation of French weakness.
Russian withdrawal following disagreement and failed cooperation left Austria exposed to renewed French campaigning.

field_changes.before: The constitutional design alone did not doom the Directory; political actors never allowed it to function freely, yet their fears of anti-constitutional extremes were not baseless.
field_changes.after: The constitution was not given a genuine trial: political manipulation and rejection of legitimate organized opposition destroyed its credibility. The Directors failed to organize their own centre and alternately suppressed parties. Yet royalist and Jacobin threats were real; critique of repression is not proof that either extreme would tolerate pluralism.

before: Party politics -- rejection under the Directory
after: Party politics -- rejection under the Directory
Royalist and Jacobin intolerance of opposition

field_changes.before: The indirect electoral lists, Senate, Tribunate, Legislative Body, Council of State, three Consuls, and dominant First Consul established after Brumaire.
field_changes.after: The Year VIII constitution retained nominal suffrage through successive lists of eligible citizens while the Senate selected legislators. The Tribunate debated without voting,the Legislative Body voted without debate,and executive proposals came through the Council of State. The First Consul dominated the executive. Implementation preceded a manipulated plebiscite.

field_changes.before: The constitution preserved a thin representative facade while concentrating initiative and effective authority in the executive, especially the First Consul.
field_changes.after: Lists of eligibility did not let citizens choose their rulers. Divided legislative functions and lack of initiative preserved a representative appearance with little control; mass abstention and inflated returns preclude treating nominal ratification as genuine popular authorization.

before.evidence_summary: Indirect lists replace direct electoral control; a Senate selects legislators, while separate chambers discuss and vote without legislative initiative.
The constitution is implemented before a manipulated plebiscite and retains only mutilated remnants of the principles of 1789.

after.evidence_summary: Indirect lists replace direct electoral control; a Senate selects legislators, while separate chambers discuss and vote without legislative initiative.
The constitution operated before the plebiscite result; inflated approval and massive abstention supplied an appearance of assent rather than reliable consent.

field_changes.before: optional
field_changes.after: major

before.evidence_summary: British naval power defeats French Mediterranean ambitions and the Baltic league, yet Paul I's death and war-weariness end prospects for another coalition.
Addington's government converts peace feelers into preliminary terms after Pitt's resignation.

after.evidence_summary: British maritime successes in Egypt,Malta and Copenhagen contrasted with continental isolation. Economic discontent,the Irish union and emancipation dispute,Pitt’s resignation and Addington’s accession made negotiation possible.

field_changes.before: Reconciliation is explicitly limited by the revolutionary property settlement: return is welcomed, but restitution is excluded to secure the new social order.
field_changes.after: Personal reconciliation did not restore old ownership: purchasers of confiscated émigré and Church lands remained protected. Papal acceptance of non-return was practical and did not concede the legality of confiscation or abandon the Avignon claim.

before.evidence_summary: The emigre list closes and amnesty broadens, while the constitution guarantees that alienated emigre property remains vested in the Republic.
Later legal and religious settlements further remove doubt about revolutionary land titles.

after.evidence_summary: The emigre list closes and amnesty broadens, while the constitution guarantees that alienated emigre property remains vested in the Republic.
Later legal and religious settlements further remove doubt about revolutionary land titles.
Non-return of alienated Church lands was a precondition of negotiation; the Pope accepted the fact while retaining objections to legality.

before: Fouche, Joseph -- investigation of Infernal Machine
after: Fouche, Joseph -- investigation of Infernal Machine

field_changes.before: The political strategy of making the Consulate more reliable than monarchy or radical republicanism as guardian of property, public credit, and social stability.
field_changes.after: The Consulate made itself the guardian of revolutionary property,public credit,and social order through repeal of coercive civil measures,selective reconciliation,fiscal recovery and political repression. This protected rural national-land purchasers as well as creditors and propertied middle classes.

field_changes.before: Material security and order are treated as the regime's strongest basis of consent, achieved through selective reconciliation and coercive exclusion of radical opponents.
field_changes.after: Real legal and administrative security coexisted with exemplary violence and suppression of political liberty. Consent was conditional and social interests varied; protection of revolutionary property did not mean restoration of the old regime.

before: Middle classes -- reconciliation to the Consulate
after: Middle classes -- reconciliation to the Consulate
Revolutionary social gains versus curtailed political liberty

field_changes.before: Order improved as peace freed troops and central authority expanded, but this administrative legality coexisted with Bonaparte's disregard for legal procedure in high politics.
field_changes.after: Centralization,peace,released troops and special justice reduced disorder. This was a substantive improvement in ordinary legal security,but it coexisted with arbitrary political punishment and does not prove respect for legal safeguards in government.

after: Rule of law--ordinary life versus high politics

before: Catholic Church -- reconciliation with the Consulate
after: Catholic Church -- reconciliation with the Consulate
PiusVI--death and mistaken predictions of papal extinction

field_changes.before: The Concordat was a negotiated compromise rather than a dictated peace: it defeated both full royalist restoration and Jacobin separation while subordinating the reorganized Church to the Consular state.
field_changes.after: The Concordat was a difficult bargain,not a dictated peace. Catholicism was recognized as the majority faith without abolishing other beliefs; paid clergy,state nomination and oaths linked restored worship to government. Neither old-regime restoration nor Jacobin separation prevailed,and property transfers remained secure.

after: Catholic majority religion versus exclusive state religion
Papal authority--spiritual recognition and Gallican restraint

field_changes.before: Bonaparte's removal of critical legislators in 1802, using the Constitution's ambiguity to silence the remaining institutional resistance before enactment of the Concordat.
field_changes.after: Experienced legislators criticized treaties,special courts,Civil Code procedure and the religious settlement. Bonaparte used ambiguous constitutional renewal rules and the Senate to remove opponents before passage of the Concordat.

field_changes.before: The purge extinguished the last vestiges of free parliamentary life with little resistance, aided by a weak public attachment to representative bodies and the disappearance of an independent press.
field_changes.after: The purge extinguished the remaining independent parliamentary life. Public reaction is hard to gauge after suppression of the independent press; police reports suggest preference for stability but do not prove unanimous approval. The supplied page’s calendar year conflicts with its Year X context and is not silently corrected.

before.evidence_summary: Criticism of legislation and the Concordat leads Bonaparte to use constitutional obscurity to prepare a purge of the two chambers.
The Senate removes eighty members without resistance; restricted public evidence suggests popular preference for Bonaparte's order over ineffective politicians.

after.evidence_summary: Criticism of legislation and the Concordat prompted use of obscure renewal provisions. The page prints January1801 despite placing the event in the Year X session; preserve this internal discrepancy.
The Senate removed eighty members without resistance. Independent reporting had largely disappeared,so police accounts cannot conclusively establish public consent.

field_changes.after: Jourdan conscription law and the renewed levee en masse
major
Full activation of the Jourdan law conscripted men aged twenty to twenty-five without substitution, supplying armies but provoking resistance, desertion, and royalist recruitment.
The measure answered military necessity yet revived Year II associations and helped destabilize the countryside.

after.evidence_summary: The Councils activate universal conscription without purchased substitutes and explicitly describe it as a new mass levy.
Conscription refugees swell the planned royalist peasant force in the south-west.
A sweeping conscription measure helps trigger renewed chouannerie in the west.
Flight from recruiting officers contributes to endemic banditry until peace eases the pressure.
